title: Notifications from a stream consumer (SYNTHETIC EXAMPLE)

assumptions.text: If Redis is down when the API publishes, the notification is not lost: it is sent later from the table.
assumptions.quote: if it is not, the notification stays in the table and will be picked up later

evidence.observation: Step 4 deletes the cron job, which is the only reader of the table, so nothing picks the row up later.

assumptions.text: The provider's rate limit applies per consumer, so adding consumers adds capacity.
assumptions.quote: The email provider accepts at most one message per second per consumer
assumptions.check: Read the provider's rate-limit documentation, then send a 50-message burst from two consumers sharing one sandbox account.

assumptions.text: Duplicate notifications are rare, so consumers can skip idempotency.
assumptions.quote: Notifications are rarely duplicated, so consumers do not need to be idempotent
assumptions.check: Count notification ids published more than once over the last 30 days (group the publish log by id, keep count > 1).

assumptions.text: Load stays under 200 notifications per minute.
assumptions.quote: Peak load will stay under 200 notifications per minute

evidence.ref: psql -c "select max(n) from (select count(*) n from notifications group by date_trunc('minute', created_at)) m"
evidence.observation: peak of 118 per minute over the last 30 days (synthetic result for this example; it says nothing about campaigns)

assumptions.text: Turning the flag off is a safe rollback.
assumptions.quote: The consumer pool ships behind a flag

evidence.observation: Once the flag is on for everyone the cron job and its code are removed and sent_at is dropped, so switching the flag off restores nothing.

assumptions.text: A message acknowledged on read cannot be lost.
assumptions.quote: Each consumer acknowledges the message as soon as it is read
assumptions.check: In staging, kill -9 a consumer between the read and the provider call, then count the notifications that were never sent.

attacks.quote: the notification stays in the table and will be picked up later
attacks.attack: If Redis is down when the API publishes, the row stays in the table but nothing reads it once the cron job is gone: those notifications are never sent and nobody is told.
attacks.check: Stop Redis in staging, create 20 notifications, restart Redis and count how many are sent.

attacks.quote: acknowledges the message as soon as it is read
attacks.attack: A consumer that crashes after the read and before the provider answers loses the notification: acknowledging on read gives at-most-once delivery, and the row stays pending for ever.
attacks.check: In staging, kill -9 a consumer between the read and the provider call; count the rows still pending after 10 minutes.

attacks.quote: the cron job and its code are removed
attacks.attack: After the rollout there is no way back: the flag cannot bring back the cron job or the sent_at column, so a bad release can only be fixed by shipping another one while notifications are being lost.
attacks.check: Apply the migration in staging, then try to revert to the previous release and send a notification.

attacks.quote: accepts at most one message per second per consumer
attacks.attack: If the provider's limit applies per account instead of per consumer, the 4 consumers share it, and throttled sends that were already acknowledged are dropped.
attacks.check: Ask the provider (or read its docs) whether the limit is per API key or per connection.

attacks.quote: publishes its id to a Redis Stream called `notify`
attacks.attack: A client that repeats a request (a password-reset form, a retry loop) creates one notification per request; with no per-user limit the stream fills with duplicates and delays everyone, which is what the assumption says does not happen.
attacks.check: Send 1,000 password-reset requests for one address in staging and measure the delay of an unrelated notification.

attacks.quote: Peak load will stay under 200 notifications per minute
attacks.attack: A marketing blast of 50,000 notifications enters the stream at once; 4 consumers at one message per second need about 3.5 hours to drain it, and transactional emails wait behind it.
attacks.check: Compute N / (consumers x rate) for the largest campaign of last quarter, then load-test a 50,000-message burst in staging.

attacks.quote: so consumers do not need to be idempotent
attacks.attack: The API publishes inside the request, so any client or load-balancer retry publishes twice. Duplicates come from the publisher, not from the rarity of events, and a consumer that is not idempotent sends two emails.
attacks.check: Count notification ids published more than once over the last 30 days.
